title: Short Stuff: How California Got Its Name
summary: Short Stuff episode on the origin of the name California. Josh and Chuck open with personal banter about California and Santa Barbara, then trace theories: Arabic caliph, Greek kallos (beautiful), and caliente/calor-style hot furnace puns dismissed as silly. The main theory is Garcia Rodriguez de Montalvo's novel Las Sergas de Esplandian, a sequel to Amadis de Gaula, featuring Queen Calafia's warrior women with griffins and a mystical island paradise called California. Spanish explorers, thinking Baja California was an island, applied the name, later learning it was a peninsula, with Alta California named for the upper part. The hosts then describe a possible earlier source: the Song of Roland (French, eleventh century) mentions Califerni, linked to Calat Hammad (Qal'at Bani Hammad), a wealthy fortified town in Algeria that crumbled in the twelfth century. The hosts conclude the chain from the Algerian city to the novel to the state name is plausible but uncertain.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with personal chat about California, retiring to wine country, and Santa Barbara, then introduce the topic of where California's name came from and early failed theories.

segments.title: Caliente, caliph, and callos theories; Montalvo's novel
segments.summary: The hosts list early explanations (Arabic caliph, Greek kallos, and a hot-furnace pun) and then describe Garcia Rodriguez de Montalvo's Amadis sequel, Las Sergas de Esplandian, with Queen Calafia's warrior women and griffins.

segments.title: Spanish explorers and Baja California as an island
segments.summary: The hosts explain that the Spanish, familiar with the novel's mystical California island, named Baja California after believing it was an island; it was later found to be a peninsula, and Alta California named for the upper part.

segments.title: Song of Roland, Califerni, and Qal'at Bani Hammad
segments.summary: The hosts describe a possible earlier source: the eleventh-century Song of Roland mentions Califerni, linked to a wealthy fortified North African town (Qal'at Bani Hammad in Algeria) that crumbled in the twelfth century. They say the chain to the state name is plausible but uncertain.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Josh closes the episode and gives the iHeartRadio production credit.
